<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of Szeged <span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">{zhixiang004, siyuan.liang, rongcheng.tu, dacheng.tao}@ntu.edu.sg</span>
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Dacheng Tao
</span></span>

<span class="ltx_personname">Nanyang Technological University

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Generative world models (WMs) are increasingly used to synthesize controllable, sensor-conditioned driving videos, yet their reliance on physical priors exposes novel attack surfaces.
In this paper, we present Physical-Conditioned World Model Attack (PhysCond-WMA), the first white-box world model attack that perturbs physical-condition channels, such as HDMap embeddings and 3D-box features, to induce semantic, logic, or decision-level distortion while preserving perceptual fidelity.
PhysCond-WMA is optimized in two stages: (1) a quality-preserving guidance stage that constrains reverse-diffusion loss below a calibrated threshold, and (2) a momentum-guided denoising stage that accumulates target-aligned gradients along the denoising trajectory for stable, temporally coherent semantic shifts.
Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our approach remains effective while increasing FID by about 9% on average and FVD by about 3.9% on average.
Under the targeted attack setting, the attack success rate (ASR) reaches 0.55.
Downstream studies further show tangible risk, which using attacked videos for training decreases 3D detection performance by about 4%, and worsens open-loop planning performance by about 20%.
These findings has for the first time revealed and quantified security vulnerabilities in generative world models, driving more comprehensive security checkers.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">World models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> learn compact, structured representations of an environment and its transition dynamics, enabling agents to predict future observations, evaluate counterfactuals, and plan without exhaustive real-world interaction.
Due to the strong ability of modeling the world, world models have proven highly effective for sample-efficient policy learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>, simulation-driven evaluation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>]</cite>, and long-horizon reasoning across robotics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>, <a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>]</cite> and autonomous-driving systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>, <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite>, making world models a cornerstone for data-efficient perception and planning pipelines.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Generative world models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">65</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> have recently advanced to the point where they can produce temporally coherent, sensor-conditional videos of complex urban scenes conditioned on high-definition maps, planned trajectories, or sparse multimodal sensor data, thereby serving as controllable simulators for autonomous driving research and validation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>, <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>, <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite>.
By enabling scalable generation of corner cases and long-horizon scenarios, these models reduce reliance on costly real world collection and unlock new avenues for closed-loop testing.
However, the reliance on learned latent dynamics and imperfect conditional inputs introduces a critical vulnerability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>.
Even small, structured perturbations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> in conditions—such as slight HDMap shifts, mislabeled object boxes, or minimally perturbed trajectories—or subtle cross-modal semantic inconsistencies can be amplified through the generative pipeline, propagating over time <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite> and leading to physically implausible outcomes such as object hallucination <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>, disappearance, or causal violations.
Once such artifacts enter downstream open-loop or closed-loop planners, they can bias cost estimation, underestimate collision risks, or induce overly conservative behaviors, ultimately misguiding decision-making <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:496.9pt;"><img src="2602.18739v1/sec/cvpr2+.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/314;" width="685" height="314" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.fig1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.fig1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Adversarial attack on generative world model. By conducting white-box attacks on the generative world model, we aim to change the semantics of the generated results while preserving quality, thus achieving an adversarial attack that affects downstream tasks</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we propose <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Physical-Conditioned World Model Attack (PhysCond-WMA)</span>, a targeted adversarial attack on generative world models that manipulates the diffusion process through the model’s physical-condition channels, such as HDMap embeddings and 3D-box features, to induce semantic, logic or decision-level distortion while preserving perceptual image quality.
Physically conditioned adversarial attacks on diffusion-based world models face two key challenges:
(1) Directly optimizing HDMap and 3D-box conditions can easily push the reverse-diffusion trajectory off the data manifold, leading to noticeable artifacts and large FID/FVD degradation instead of stealthy attacks.
(2) Even in a fidelity-preserving region, the denoising update is dominated by the model’s clean prediction, so naive injection of target gradients is either too weak to change video semantics or too strong and breaks temporal consistency.
As a result, we design the two-stage method to inject small, perturbations into the physical condition layer so that they are naturally absorbed by the generator:
(1) A quality-preserving guidance stage that constrains perceptual loss to a pre-set threshold.
(2) A momentum-guided denoising optimization stage that simulates the diffusion denoising trajectory with momentum updates to robustly identify high-impact attack directions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Extensive experiments are conducted under untrageted attack and targeted attack with different victim models.
The resulting compact perturbations cause semantic, logic, or decision-relevant distortions (e.g. missing or added vehicles, lane misalignments, erroneous driving status) without a noticeable loss of image fidelity, increasing FID by about 9% and FVD by about 3.9% on average.
The attack success rate of targeted attack of PhysCond-WMA can reach 0.55 for advanced generative world models.
Experimental results on downstream detection and planner performance reveal that the attacked videos can degrade 3D detection performance by about 4% and open-loop planning performance by about 20%, proving the effectiveness of our adversarial attack <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>, <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite>.
<span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Our contributions are</span>:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first identify and systematically study the security risks of generative world models for autonomous driving, and propose <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PhysCond-WMA</span>, the first adversarial attack for this class of models.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We design a physical conditioned adversarial attack with a two-stage optimization, quality-preserving guidance and momentum-guided denoising, to attack without degrading perceptual quality.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method completes the attack with minimal image quality degradation and successfully affects downstream tasks.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>World Models in Autonomous Driving</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Generative world models for autonomous driving can be organized along two orthogonal axes: generation paradigm and conditioning priors.
Physically constrained diffusion for multi-view generation methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>, <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>, <a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">65</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> use conditions such as HD maps, BEV layouts, 3D boxes, or trajectories to synthesize controllable, cross-view consistent driving videos.
DriveDreamer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite> leveraged diffusion with a two-stage pipeline to encode traffic structure and predict futures from real-world data.
On this basis, in order to enhance controllable condition generation and multi view modeling capabilities, DriveDreamer2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite> added LLM-to-trajectory and HDMap interfaces, and unified multi camera modeling to improve spatiotemporal consistency.
Under this architecture, diffusion models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite> have been widely applied to drive temporally-consistent, multi-view controllable video generation with strong structural prior conditions, ensuring geometric and semantic stability through explicit cross view alignment and long-term consistency mechanisms.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Secondly, generative world models unify video, actions, and language via sequence modeling or latent diffusion.
GAIA-1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> adopts discrete sequence modeling for controllable driving video synthesis, while GAIA-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite> advances to controllable multi-camera latent diffusion with broader geographic diversity. and tighter alignment to structured priors, an industrial path toward world models and control priors.
Moreover, WoVoGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite> utilizes voxel and volumetric abstractions to tighten the geometry–time coupling, improving physical interpretability.
In order to further enhance the perception and temporal modeling capabilities of end-to-end models, LAW <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite> directly introduces the world model into the latent space and predicts the potential features of future scenes based on the current visual features and the vehicle trajectory.
However, these methods rely on multimodal physical conditions to enhance the perceptual ability of the world model while also increasing the risk of attacks against these physical conditions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Diffusion-Based Adversarial Attacks</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Due to the limited research on attacks against world models, we focus on the adversarial attack <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> of diffusion models, the core structure of generative world models.
AdvDiff <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> generates unrestricted adversarial examples by injecting classifier gradient based adversarial guidance into the reverse diffusion sampling process, yielding realistic high quality attacks that outperform prior unrestricted methods.
AdvDiffVLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> modifies the reverse-time diffusion score via adaptive ensemble gradients to efficiently synthesize natural, unrestricted, targeted adversarial examples that transfer across VLMs.
Similarly, AdvDiffuser <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> injects adversarial semantics by applying Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> to the reverse diffusion process, but significantly reduces the quality of the generated results.
In this regard, Adversarial-Guided Diffusion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>]</cite> injects target semantics in the final few steps of reverse diffusion and aligns the denoising trajectory with momentum, thereby achieving efficient, transferable, and anti-purification targeted unconstrained attacks with high fidelity.
These methods lay the foundations of a novel adversarial paradigm against world models: launching attacks against the physical laws of the world model.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Preliminaries</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Generative World Model</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Leveraging diffusion’s training stability and efficient latent-space modeling, conditional diffusion has become a standard backbone for generative world models, enabling explicit injection of physical priors and thereby improving both perception quality and decision-making.
Typical physical priors <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> include HDMaps, 3D bounding boxes, and BEV trajectory/layout representations.
HDMaps are centimeter and lane-level semantic maps for autonomous driving that encode road geometry, lane boundaries and centerlines, crosswalks, stop lines, traffic lights and signs, drivable areas, and their topological relations.
3D bounding boxes record, in a global coordinate frame, each object’s translation <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y,z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y,z)</annotation></semantics></math>, size <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(w,l,h)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(w,l,h)</annotation></semantics></math>, orientation (quaternion/heading), and often velocity vector.
These priors help maintain coherent positions, headings, and speeds of interactive agents during generation.
Bird’s-eye view (BEV) is a ground-plane feature representation obtained by lifting multi-camera features into 3D and splatting them onto a bird’s-eye grid, providing a unified spatial reference that aligns maps, objects, planning, and kinematic reasoning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The diffusion model mainly includes two steps: forward denoising and conditional reverse denoising.
Let <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> denote a ground-truth video frame in latent space. The forward process adds noise as Eq.(<a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3.1 Generative World Model ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="q(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0})=\mathcal{N}\!\bigl(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\mathbf{x}_{0},\;(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\mathbf{I}\bigr),\quad t=1,\dots,T" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mpadded style="width:0.798em;" width="0.798em"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi></mpadded><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msqrt><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></msqrt><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>𝐈</mi><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0})=\mathcal{N}\!\bigl(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\mathbf{x}_{0},\;(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\mathbf{I}\bigr),\quad t=1,\dots,T</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\alpha}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\alpha}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as in DDPM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>. The reverse process generates conditionally on physical priors
<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> and input conditions <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> (text, images, videos), as depicted in Eq.(<a href="#S3.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 3.1 Generative World Model ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>)</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},R,C\right)=\mathcal{N}\!\big(\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,R,C),\,\sigma_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I}\big)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.798em;" width="0.798em"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐈</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},R,C\right)=\mathcal{N}\!\big(\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,R,C),\,\sigma_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I}\big)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t},\,t,\,R,\,C\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t},\,t,\,R,\,C\right)</annotation></semantics></math> is the diffusion noise predictor. The loss function of diffusion model is depicted as Eq.(<a href="#S3.E3" title="Equation 3 ‣ 3.1 Generative World Model ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{0},\;\epsilon_{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,I),\;t,\;C}\!\left[\big\lVert\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\,t,\,R,\,C)\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>∼</mo></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{0},\;\epsilon_{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,I),\;t,\;C}\!\left[\big\lVert\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\,t,\,R,\,C)\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.4" class="ltx_p">Meanwhile, video diffusion introduces temporal attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite>, 3D spatiotemporal U-Net <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>, and cascaded spatiotemporal super-resolution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite> on the basis of image diffusion to maintain long-range consistency. In Video Diffusion Models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>, high fidelity and long-term video synthesis are achieved through a cascade paradigm of basic generation and spatiotemporal super-resolution.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18739v1/sec/cvpr3.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/251;" width="685" height="251" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overall framework of PhysCond-WMA.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Problem Definition</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We adopt a white-box, inference-time threat model: the attacker can access and utilize the victim model’s pretrained weights and gradient information, but is not allowed to train or fine-tune the model parameters.
For a generative world model, the output of the model can be represented as Eq.(<a href="#S3.E4" title="Equation 4 ‣ 3.2 Problem Definition ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{V}=\{\mathbf{x}_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}=\mathcal{WM}(R,C)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐕</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{V}=\{\mathbf{x}_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}=\mathcal{WM}(R,C)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where M represents the frame rate, R represents the physical conditions, and C represents the input multimodal conditions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, during the attack, the goal of the attacker is to create a subtle perturbation <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta</annotation></semantics></math>, allowing the world model adversarial attack to change semantics either directionally or non directionally while maintaining the quality of the generated results.
In order to better achieve the goal, the perturbation is applied to the physical conditions, making it more controllable while satisfying the covert attack, as depicted in Eq.(<a href="#S3.E5" title="Equation 5 ‣ 3.2 Problem Definition ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{V}^{att}=\{\mathbf{x}_{m}^{att}\}_{m=1}^{M}=\mathcal{WM}(R+\delta,C^{*})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐕</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{V}^{att}=\{\mathbf{x}_{m}^{att}\}_{m=1}^{M}=\mathcal{WM}(R+\delta,C^{*})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the injected perturbation, and the <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the targeted attack conditions.
Therefore, during the attack, although the input modality may be different from the target modality, encoding is needed to align the two in the latent space.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">To formalize the attack objective, we decompose the adversary’s goals into three parts: ①Control perturbation magnitude to ensure the attack is imperceptible. ②Preserve perceptual and geometric fidelity of generated results. ③Align the target in the denoising trajectory.
We pose the attacker’s optimization as a minimization over the physical-condition perturbation <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta</annotation></semantics></math>, as depicted in Eq.(<a href="#S3.E6" title="Equation 6 ‣ 3.2 Problem Definition ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E6X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E6X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\delta(t)=\arg\min_{\delta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><munder><mi>min</mi><mi>δ</mi></munder></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\delta(t)=\arg\min_{\delta}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E6X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\lambda_{R}\|\delta\|_{2}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\lambda_{R}\|\delta\|_{2}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E6X.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\;+" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>+</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\;+</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E6X.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\lambda_{L}\,\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t}^{att})\big]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo mathsize="1.200em">,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\lambda_{L}\,\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t}^{att})\big]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E6Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E6Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\;-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\;-</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E6Xa.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\lambda_{tar}\,\mathcal{A}\big(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{att},C^{*})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\lambda_{tar}\,\mathcal{A}\big(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{att},C^{*})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright" colspan="3"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{R}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{L}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{tar}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{tar}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes scale factors to control these three parts. <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}</annotation></semantics></math> is depicted in Eq.(<a href="#S3.E3" title="Equation 3 ‣ 3.1 Generative World Model ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math> aligns the semantic similarity between the target <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> and denoising latent <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{t}^{att}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{t}^{att}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Approach</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we propose <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">PhysCond-WMA</span>, a two-stage adversarial attack that injects a compact noise perturbation into the diffusion process, optimized in two stages: ① a quality-preserving guidance stage and ② a momentum-guided denoising optimization stage, as shown in Fig.<a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Generative World Model ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Quality-preserving Guidance Stage</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the reverse diffusion steps, <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the input of the noise predictor <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> for gradual denoising steps, as shown in Eq.(<a href="#S3.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 3.1 Generative World Model ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). Therefore, the single denoising step from t to t-1 is depicted as Eq.(<a href="#S4.E7" title="Equation 7 ‣ 4.1 Quality-preserving Guidance Stage ‣ 4 Approach ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>).</p>
<table id="S4.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{t-1}=\mathrm{denoise}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t},\;\epsilon_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:3.180em;" width="3.180em"><mi>denoise</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{t-1}=\mathrm{denoise}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t},\;\epsilon_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">In the quality-preserving guidance stage, we preserve perceptual fidelity while gently moving the reverse denoising trajectory away from the clean flow when attacking the reverse diffusion.
Therefore, we intend to add small perturbations to guide the generation of the image while retaining the original diffusion.
Because reverse diffusion is fundamentally sampling guided by the score field, there is no guarantee of monotonic loss decrease across steps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>; consequently, merely injecting small perturbations can trap the trajectory in a local minima which undermines the adversarial attack.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Concretely, we enlarge a diffusion-space discrepancy to escape the local basin around the clean video, while keeping the state on-manifold to preserve realism.
As a result, a small corrective perturbation is added in the reverse diffusion which directly reduces the diffusion diffusion loss, as depicted in Eq.(<a href="#S4.E8" title="Equation 8 ‣ 4.1 Quality-preserving Guidance Stage ‣ 4 Approach ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>)</p>
<table id="S4.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\epsilon}_{t}=\epsilon_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)+\alpha_{A}\,\cdot\,\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\text{att}}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.392em">⋅</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msub><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext>att</mtext></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\epsilon}_{t}=\epsilon_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)+\alpha_{A}\,\cdot\,\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\text{att}}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{A}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the scale factor of the gradient of the loss function.
Because the clean denoising <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\epsilon}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\epsilon}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> dominates each update, the global trend of <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}</annotation></semantics></math> is naturally decreasing, which makes the next stage with a quality-preserving output.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">With the attack starting from reverse step T, we terminate the first stage at the first step <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> that satisfies the quality-preserving fidelity criterion, as depicted in Eq.(<a href="#S4.E9" title="Equation 9 ‣ 4.1 Quality-preserving Guidance Stage ‣ 4 Approach ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>).</p>
<table id="S4.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta=\min\!\left\{t\in\{T,\dots,1\}\;\middle|\;\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}(x_{t};\,x_{t}^{\text{att}})&lt;\tau\right\}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.653em;" width="1.653em"><mi>min</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="true">|</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext>att</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta=\min\!\left\{t\in\{T,\dots,1\}\;\middle|\;\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}(x_{t};\,x_{t}^{\text{att}})&lt;\tau\right\}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where the threshold <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> is determined by ablation experiments in <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>.
An overly large <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> relaxes the constraint too early, leading to poor image quality and semantic blur.
An overly small <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> keeps the trajectory overly coupled to the clean anchor, making it difficult for the next stage of our attack to converge towards the target direction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, the quality-preserving guidance stage constrains <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}</annotation></semantics></math> with a threshold <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> and injects small perturbations, so that the denoising trajectory while remaining on the data manifold.
This provides a stable and optimizable starting point for the subsequent momentum-guided target alignment.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18739v1/sec/cvpr5.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/257;" width="685" height="257" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Visualization of untargeted and targeted PhysCond-WMA</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Denoising Optimization Stage</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this stage, once the reverse diffusion process has converged and the loss <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}</annotation></semantics></math> reaches the predefined threshold, the inference continues toward the target semantics.
To achieve this, we employ SSCD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite> to quantify the semantic consistency between the denoised result and the target representation, allowing us to guide the diffusion process to maximize their semantic alignment.
We focus on the case where both C and R are single images. In settings where multiple conditioning signals are used and a subset of them can be used as the target, the alignment should be minimized with the target subset.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The key challenge lies in the fact that the denoising update is still dominated by the intrinsic prediction of the model <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon(\mathbf{x}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon(\mathbf{x}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, which naturally drives the process toward clean reconstruction.
Thus, the optimization must accumulate target-oriented updates that are sufficiently strong to alter the semantic trajectory, while simultaneously ensuring that <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}</annotation></semantics></math> does not increase, thereby maintaining visual fidelity and temporal coherence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">As <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon(\mathbf{x}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon(\mathbf{x}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> gradually decreases with each reverse diffusion step, the model becomes increasingly sensitive to abrupt gradient changes.
Directly updating along the raw target gradient may thus cause unstable behavior and lead to poor temporal consistency in the generated video.
To mitigate this issue, we introduce an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite> mechanism that accumulates the target-directed gradients over time into a smooth and coherent semantic offset trajectory, as depicted in Eq.(<a href="#S4.E10" title="Equation 10 ‣ 4.2 Denoising Optimization Stage ‣ 4 Approach ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>).</p>
<table id="S4.E10" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S4.E10X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E10X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\tilde{\epsilon}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\tilde{\epsilon}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E10X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\lambda{\epsilon}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\lambda{\epsilon}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E10X.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\;+" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>+</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\;+</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E10X.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle(1-\lambda)\!\left[\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\mathcal{A}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{att},\,C^{*}\right)\right." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>λ</mi><mpadded style="width:0.219em;" width="0.219em"><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mpadded><mo>[</mo><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msub><mpadded style="width:0.628em;" width="0.628em"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mpadded><mo>(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mi>C</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle(1-\lambda)\!\left[\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\mathcal{A}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{att},\,C^{*}\right)\right.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.E10Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E10Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\;-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\;-</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E10Xa.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\beta\,\cdot\,\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\text{att}}\right)\left.\vphantom{\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}}\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0.392em" rspace="0.392em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><mo>(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mtext>att</mtext></msup><mo>)</mo><mo>]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\beta\,\cdot\,\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\text{att}}\right)\left.\vphantom{\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}}\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright" colspan="3"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the momentum factor with <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda\in\left(0,1\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda\in\left(0,1\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the semantic alignment model, which is SSCD in our case.
When the attack is untargeted, the perturbation is depicted as Eq.(<a href="#S4.E11" title="Equation 11 ‣ 4.2 Denoising Optimization Stage ‣ 4 Approach ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>).</p>
<table id="S4.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\epsilon}_{t}=\lambda{\epsilon}_{t}+(1-\lambda)\,\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\text{att}}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.337em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msub><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi><mtext>att</mtext></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\epsilon}_{t}=\lambda{\epsilon}_{t}+(1-\lambda)\,\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\text{att}}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.4" class="ltx_p">This temporal aggregation suppresses short-term fluctuations in the update direction, ensuring that the semantic transition toward the target remains stable while preserving both visual quality and spatio-temporal coherence in the final video results.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Attack Pipeline and Implementation Details</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Fig.<a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Generative World Model ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, the PhysCond-WMA framework integrates both quality-preserving and target-guided stages within a unified diffusion pipeline.
The attack operates in the latent video space while conditioning on physical priors R(HDMap, 3D-box) and input target contexts <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> (images, text, or multimodal prompts).
During inference, the clean reverse-diffusion path is duplicated into an adversarial branch where perturbations are injected under loss-threshold control. The Stage 1 module constrains the diffusion loss below <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> to maintain perceptual fidelity, while Stage 2 introduces a momentum-guided update that aggregates gradients aligned with a semantic target, steering the denoising trajectory toward the desired shift.
The framework outputs three categories of results, including semantic level, logic level and decision level distortions.
<span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For detailed definitions, please refer to section 5.1</span>
Together, these modules form an end-to-end controllable adversarial pipeline capable of precise, temporally consistent attacks on generative world models.
<span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">More details about the algorithm can be found in Supplementary Materials.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dataset and Model.</span>
The experimental dataset used is the nuScenes dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, consisting of 850 actual driving videos, including 700 training videos and 150 validation videos.
Each video is approximately 20 seconds long and has a frame rate of 12 frames per second, including cameras from six surround perspectives, totaling over 1 million video frames.
At the same time, the dataset provides physical conditions for sampling key frames, including HDMap, 3D Box, driving status, and other conditions.
For targeted attacks, the target comes from video frames in the validation set, and the attack is guided by changing the semantics in the image, such as adding vehicles, pedestrians, modifying traffic light information.
We use SDXL-inpainting 1.0 model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite> to generate targets.
<span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">More details about targets can be found in Supplementary materials.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method on Drivedreamer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite> and Drivedreamer2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite> autonomous driving generative world models.
We train DriveDreamer from scratch following the official recipe, whereas DriveDreamer2 is evaluated using the released pretrained checkpoints.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation Metrics.</span>
We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of our proposed method, including the effectiveness of the attack and impact on downstream tasks.
The evaluation of attack effectiveness includes the quality of the generated results and Attack Success Rate.
We utilized frame-wise Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> and Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite> to evaluate the generation quality, where the evaluated image is resized to 448 × 256.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Main results</h3>

<figure id="S5.F4.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:496.9pt;"><img src="2602.18739v1/sec/cvpr4.png" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/433;" width="685" height="433" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F4.fig1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S5.F4.fig1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Visualization of PhysCond-WMA. GPT-5 determines attack failure, while human determines attack success.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To quantify Attack Success Rate (ASR), for which no established metric exists in world model attacks, we introduce a set of evaluation criteria and use GPT-5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite> and human as evaluators.
Each video is evaluated along three levels: semantic level, logical level and decision level.
(1) Semantic level: recognizability of key traffic elements such as vehicles, pedestrians, traffic lights/signs, lane markings, and other road-relevant entities;
(2) Logical level: temporal/physical coherence such as smooth ego/object motion; absence of object teleportation or disappearance; no implausible spatial placements;
(3) Decision level: appropriateness of responses to risk such as obstacles, pedestrians, red lights.
Each dimension is scored from the set <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,1]</annotation></semantics></math>, where larger values indicate greater degradation.
As a result, the final score <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> can be depicted as <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}}s_{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}}s_{d}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}=\{\mathbf{sem},\mathbf{log},\mathbf{dec}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>𝐬𝐞𝐦</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐥𝐨𝐠</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐝𝐞𝐜</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}=\{\mathbf{sem},\mathbf{log},\mathbf{dec}\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
If <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}&gt;0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}&gt;0.5</annotation></semantics></math>, the attack successes.
Each experiment consists of 100 generated results, and the number of successful attacks is calculated as ASR.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the evaluation of Human ASR, we recruited 20 adult volunteers with driving experience to score the generated videos based on the same evaluation criteria as GPT.
Each person evaluated 20 videos, and each video was evaluated by at least two people.
After statistical analysis, Human ASR was determined.
<span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">More details about evaluation criteria can be found in Supplementary Materials.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For downstream impact, we evaluate the generated results on 3D object detection and open-loop planning.
Among them, FCOS3D <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite> is selected as baselines for 3D object detection, and ST-P3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> and VAD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite> are selected as baselines for open-loop planning to measure the driving trajectory in the next three seconds.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Implementation details.</span>
In our proposed method, we set <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{A}=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{A}=0.1</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=0.9</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.6</annotation></semantics></math>.
Based on preliminary experiments, we choose <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.15</annotation></semantics></math> as the threshold to terminate the quality-preserving stage.
The number of diffusion steps is 25.
The resolution of a single lens in the generated results is 448 × 256.
In our experiments, we set image condition as the DriveDreamer generation mode.</p>
</div>
