<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Tab.<a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows the attack performance of PhysCond-WMA on different generative world models, including both untargeted and targeted attacks.
The results indicate that PhysCond-WMA can attack while maintaining visual quality.
Notably, on different models, the Human ASR is higher than the GPT’s.
We attribute this gap to the attack mechanism: perturbations maintain single-frame fidelity yet induce temporally accumulated semantic shifts that alter driving semantics.
As illustrated in Fig.<a href="#S5.F4.fig1" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Main results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, frames remain visually plausible while the video-level meaning changes
For example, the oncoming vehicle switches from a bus to a truck.
GPT-based assessors—biased toward appearance cues and short-horizon reasoning.
Therefore under-report these “visually normal but behaviorally abnormal” samples, whereas human raters detect cross-frame semantic and causal violations.
This divergence evidences the stealthiness and effectiveness of PhysCond-WMA.
In large-scale pipelines, manual auditing is costly, and automated screening using LLMs further increases the risk that such covert attacks remain undetected.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:496.9pt;"><img src="2602.18739v1/sec/cvpr8.png" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/283;" width="685" height="283" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F5.fig1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S5.F5.fig1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Ablation study on loss function threshold <math id="S5.F5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">By comparing untargeted and targeted attack, we found that PhysCond-WMA achieved an improvement in ASR of about 60% in targeted attack.
This indicates that our method can effectively guide reverse diffusion towards the target direction, ensuring both result quality and attack effectiveness.
Fig.<a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Quality-preserving Guidance Stage ‣ 4 Approach ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the results of both untargeted targeted attacks.
Result (A) displays a generation of rainy driving scene, while after attacking, the original green light has been distorted into red light.
Result (B) displays a generation of a daytime driving scene, with a target vehicle in the first frame.
PhysCond-WMA successfully guides the generation of the video, causing a change in the speed of the target vehicle, and the target disappeared in the last frame, which violates basic logic.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Meanwhile, note that the Human ASR on DriveDreamer2 improves over DriveDreamer by 28% for the untargeted setting and 34.1% for the targeted setting.
Because PhysCond-WMA is a white-box attack, its effectiveness correlates with the model’s conditional coupling strength and temporal modeling capability.
In stronger generators, small perturbations on physical conditions propagate stably along the diffusion–denoising chain and gradually accumulate into cross-frame semantic shifts.
As shown in Fig.<a href="#S3.E4" title="Equation 4 ‣ 3.2 Problem Definition ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, single frames look normal, yet the video semantics change from bus to truck, which substantially raises Human ASR.
This also explains why targeted attacks achieve a higher success rate.
Goal-aligned gradients are more easily amplified and temporally preserved by strong spatiotemporal priors, boosting attack efficiency while causing only minor quality changes, thus remaining more invisible to appearance-biased, short-horizon automatic assessors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Tab.<a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Main results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.2 Main results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> show the impact of attack results on downstream tasks, including using the results as synthetically augmented data for 3D detection training and open-loop planning performance.
In 3D detection, we add a total of 800 frames from 100 attacked videos into the training set.
The results show that compared to clean data augmentation, mean average precision (mAP) decreased by 1.1 and 1.3, and nuScenes Detection Score (NDS) decreased by 0.7 and 1.9, with DriveDreamer and DriveDreamer2, respectively.
These results confirm that, despite similar perceptual quality, PhysCond-WMA introduces semantic and physical inconsistencies that contaminate the training distribution and systematically harm downstream detection ,degrading both mAP and NDS across models.
The larger drops on DriveDreamer2 corroborate our earlier observation that stronger generators are more vulnerable.
In open-loop planning performance, the L2 displacement error (L2 Avg.) of PhysCond-WMA increases from 0.29 to 0.33 compared to the clean DriveDreamer representing a relative increase of 13.8%.
The collision rate increased from 0.15% to 0.19%, a relative increase increase of 26.7%.
This indicates that our method worsens the collision rate while perturbing the trajectory, demonstrating the impact of attack results on downstream tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Ablation Study</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To demonstrate the effectiveness of our design method, we conduct ablation experiments on the loss function threshold <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> set for stopping the first stage of the attack.
Moreover, we ablate the two attack stages and the conditional layers of the PhysCond-WMA
We use DriveDreamer2 in our ablation experiments as the victim model, as it has better experimental results and Human ASR is used as the evaluation metric.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Loss function threshold <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math></span>.
Fig.<a href="#S5.F5.fig1" title="Figure 5 ‣ 5.2 Main results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> illustrates the ASR and FVD with different values of <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>.
By comparison, it can be concluded that as <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> gradually increases, the FVD of the generated results gradually increases, and the image quality of the generated results gradually deteriorates.
When <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.10</annotation></semantics></math>, although FVD is minimized, the loss function is prone to getting stuck in local minima, which is not conducive to the next stage of attack.
When <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.20</annotation></semantics></math>, the diffusion process is incomplete and the quality of the generated results cannot be guaranteed.
Therefore, after the next stage of attack, the generated results cannot converge to the target, and the ASR is very low.
As a result, in order to balance quality of the generated results and the effectiveness of attack, we set <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.15</annotation></semantics></math>.
<br class="ltx_break"></p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="S5.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Ablation study of attack stage.</span></figcaption>

</figure>
<figure id="S5.F6.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:496.9pt;"><img src="2602.18739v1/sec/cvpr10.png" id="S5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/381;" width="685" height="381" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F6.fig1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S5.F6.fig1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Visualization of ablation study of attack stage.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Effect of two stages.</span>
Tab.<a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> illustrates the ASR and FVD with different attack stages.
To ensure fair comparison, we conduct stage-wise ablations: when only one stage is executed, all remaining steps follow the standard reverse diffusion without additional perturbations.
Results show that only using quality-preserving stage quickly attenuates perturbations along the denoising chain, thus largely maintaining perceptual quality, but ASR drops by 87.5% with the untargeted attack and 94.5% with the targeted attack, indicating that, without the alignment of stage 2, the attack cannot accumulate enough semantic shift.
Conversely, by only using the momentum-guided optimization stage, FVD increases by 13.5% and 23.4% relative to only using the first stage, confirming the strong quality-preserving effect of stage 1.
Meanwhile, ASR still decreases by 81.3% and 80% compared to the entire two-stage method.
These results imply that stage 1 not only safeguards fidelity but also, under an appropriate thresholds <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, constrains and shapes the denoising trajectory, providing a stable and optimizable starting point for targeted updates of stage 2.
For example, as shown in Fig.<a href="#S5.F6.fig1" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, in PhysCond-WMA, the attack occurs as a semantic change of the object between frames.
When using only the first stage, the attack fails by preserving quality without semantic changes, and when only using phase two, the failure is a result of the low-quality output, corresponding with our earlier analysis.
As a result, the two stages are complementary and indispensable: stage 1 stabilizes the trajectory and preserves quality, while stage 2 injects target-semantic deviations and steers convergence.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Physical conditions.</span>
Tab.<a href="#S5.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> compares single-channel physical conditions (HDMap or 3D Box) with joint conditions.
By comparison, PhysCond-WMA achieves higher ASR than only using HDMap or 3D Box conditions, showing an increase of 52.4% and 28.0% in the untargeted setting and 37.5% and 41.0% in the targeted setting, while keeping perceptual quality comparable.
These results indicate that HDMap constrains road topology and 3D Box anchors objects in the frame.
As shown in Fig.<a href="#S5.F7.fig1" title="Figure 7 ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, when onlt the HDMap is attacked, the road information is affected, leading to generate wrong road sign.
By contrast, when only the 3D box is attacked, the object semantics are changed, leading to unreasonable appearance.
Our method perturbs both physical conditions, ensuring a successful attack.</p>
</div>

<td id="S5.T5.5.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.65pt 8.0pt;"><span id="S5.T5.5.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">FVD<math id="S5.T5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math></span></td>
<td id="S5.T5.5.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.65pt 8.0pt;"><span id="S5.T5.5.1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">ASR(Human)<math id="S5.T5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math></span></td>
<td id="S5.T5.5.1.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.65pt 8.0pt;"><span id="S5.T5.5.1.2.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">FVD<math id="S5.T5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math></span></td>
<td id="S5.T5.5.1.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.65pt 8.0pt;"><span id="S5.T5.5.1.2.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">ASR(Human)<math id="S5.T5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math></span></td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T5.5.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S5.T5.5.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.65pt 8.0pt;"><span id="S5.T5.5.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">HDMap</span></td>
<td id="S5.T5.5.1.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.65pt 8.0pt;"><span id="S5.T5.5.1.3.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">76.9</span></td>
<td id="S5.T5.5.1.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.65pt 8.0pt;"><span id="S5.T5.5.1.3.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">0.21</span></td>
<td id="S5.T5.5.1.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.65pt 8.0pt;"><span id="S5.T5.5.1.3.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">77.1</span></td>

</span></div>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusions and Future Work</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper proposes <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">PhysCond-WMA</span>, the first white-box attack on generative world models that perturbs physical-condition channels to induce temporally coherent semantic shifts while preserving perceptual quality.
Our method demonstrates the vulnerability of generative world models under conditional perturbations, and experimental results confirm that downstream tasks are successfully impacted.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We aim to raise awareness of world model safety, and develop a multi-dimension safety checker that goes beyond fidelity metrics to evaluate generated data via perceptual, temporal, physics and policy compliance dimensions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Limitations:</span>
(1)The effectiveness of this method has been verified in image targets as input condition, but the attack effect on multimodal targets such as video and text still needs to be explored.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">(2)Due to the lack of unified standards for world model safety, our evaluation methodology does not represent a complete criteria, only a valuable step towards it.


<span id="S6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Algorithm of PhysCond-WMA</h2>

<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Target Generation</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We employ an SDXL-based inpainting model to inject additional objects into driving-scene images.
Specifically, given a clean frame, we first define a binary mask over the target region and construct a text prompt describing the object to be inserted.
Next, we feed the original image, the mask, and the text prompt into the SDXL inpainting pipeline, which keeps the unmasked area fixed while regenerating only the masked region under the textual condition so that the new object is geometrically and photometrically consistent with the surrounding scene.
Finally, we decode and composite the inpainted result with the original image to obtain edited frames where additional vehicles or traffic signs are seamlessly integrated, which are then used as targets for our experiments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The target examples is shown in Fig.<a href="#S8.F8.fig1" title="Figure 8 ‣ 8 Target Generation ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>.
For example, the prompt of (a) is :<span id="S8.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A realistic daytime campus road scene in front of a modern building. Add a large yellow rectangular traffic warning sign in the left foreground on the sidewalk, mounted on a silver pole, with the black text ”SLOW DOWN” in bold capital letters. Keep the original pedestrians and background unchanged, natural lighting, high-resolution photo.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The prompt of (b) is :<span id="S8.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A realistic daytime city street scene with red-brick buildings on both sides and a crosswalk ahead. Add a silver mid-size sedan driving away from the camera in the center of the nearest lane, aligned with the yellow lane markings, slight motion blur on the wheels. Keep the pedestrians, traffic lights, buildings, and background cars unchanged, match the original lighting, color tone and perspective of the photo.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S8.F8.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:496.9pt;"><img src="2602.18739v1/sec/supp1.png" id="S8.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/371;" width="685" height="371" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S8.F8.fig1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="S8.F8.fig1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Visualization of target generation.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S9" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">9 </span>ASR Evaluation</h2>

<div id="S9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we provide a detailed introduction to two different ASR evaluation methods, including GPT and Human.</p>
</div>
<section id="S9.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">9.1 </span>ASR(GPT-5)</h3>

<div id="S9.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Firstly, we process the results and extract all frames of the generated video, including multi-views.
Using all frames without subsampling, a rater assigns per-view scores on three axes with higher values indicating worse quality/safety: 
<br class="ltx_break">(1) Semantic Level: whether key traffic elements, including vehicles, pedestrians, traffic lights/signs, lane markings, drivable area, remain clearly discernible. At the same time, the frame should be clear and recognizable; 
<br class="ltx_break">(2)Logical Level: absence of discontinuities such as pop-in/out, teleportation, implausible scale/pose changes, or placement in physically impossible locations. For example, a person sppears in the middle of the road; 
<br class="ltx_break">(3)Decision Level: whether the ego-vehicle’s behavior is appropriate when risks occur (obstacles, pedestrians, slow/lead vehicles, red lights).
For example, timely slowing, stopping, headway keeping, or reasonable lane change.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Each axis uses the discrete set 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1, where 0 = best and 1 = worst. If no salient risk appears throughout a clip, <math id="S9.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{\text{dec}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mtext>dec</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{\text{dec}}</annotation></semantics></math> = 0.2 by convention; if frames are insufficient to judge a dimension, 0.6 may be used as an “uncertain” placeholder. We average each axis across the six views to obtain <math id="S9.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{s}_{\text{sem}},\ \bar{s}_{\text{log}},\ \bar{s}_{\text{dec}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mtext>sem</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mtext>log</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mtext>dec</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{s}_{\text{sem}},\ \bar{s}_{\text{log}},\ \bar{s}_{\text{dec}}</annotation></semantics></math> and report the overall score <math id="S9.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S=(\bar{s}_{\text{sem}}+\ \bar{s}_{\text{log}}+\ \bar{s}_{\text{dec}})/3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mtext>sem</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0.722em">+</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mtext>log</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0.722em">+</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mtext>dec</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S=(\bar{s}_{\text{sem}}+\ \bar{s}_{\text{log}}+\ \bar{s}_{\text{dec}})/3</annotation></semantics></math> on a 0–1 scale. An attack is deemed successful if <math id="S9.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S&gt;0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S&gt;0.5</annotation></semantics></math>. The prompt for ASR(GPT) is shown in Fig.<a href="#S9.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ 9.1 ASR(GPT-5) ‣ 9 ASR Evaluation ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S9.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18739v1/sec/supp2.png" id="S9.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:685/783;" width="685" height="783" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S9.F9.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 9</span>: </span><span id="S9.F9.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The prompt of ASR(GPT) Evaluator.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S9.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">9.2 </span>ASR(Human)</h3>

<div id="S9.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given that automated metrics may not accurately reflect human judgments of attack success, we also incorporate a manual evaluation process to compare the effectiveness of GPT-5’s assessments with human judgments.
We recruit 20 volunteers for the assessment, all of whom must be at least 18 years old, in good physical and mental health, and free from conditions such as heart disease or vasovagal syncope.
Before the assessment, we present definitions and examples of each level of attack success to the volunteers.
Volunteers view full videos on 22-24 inch monitors.
Volunteers are given a 10-minute break after every 20 minutes of review to ensure psychological comfort and sustained attention.
Each video receives evaluations from at least two volunteers. Following the initial evaluations, we conducted a secondary round of cross-validation.
The detailed survey questionnaire is shown in Fig.<a href="#S9.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ 9.2 ASR(Human) ‣ 9 ASR Evaluation ‣ When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S9.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18739v1/sec/supp3.png" id="S9.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:685/882;" width="685" height="882" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S9.F10.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 10</span>: </span><span id="S9.F10.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The survey questionnaire of ASR(Human) Evaluator.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S10" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">10 </span>Results</h2>

<div id="S10.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S10.p1.1" class="ltx_p">More attacked results are provided in the ZIP file.
The reasons why each result is considered a successful attack are as follows:
<br class="ltx_break">(1)Wrongly generated the speed of movement while waiting for the red light.
<br class="ltx_break">(2)Incorrect semantics were generated, and the opposing vehicle changed from a bus to a truck.
<br class="ltx_break">(3)Wrong decision, not slowing down at the intersection.
<br class="ltx_break">(4)Wrongly generated the speed of movement while waiting for the red light.
<br class="ltx_break">(5)Wrongly generated the speed of movement while waiting for the red light.
<br class="ltx_break">(6)Incorrect semantic generation, loss of pedestrian crossing lines on the road surface.
<br class="ltx_break">(7)Incorrect semantic generation, resulting in the car being turned into a truck.
<br class="ltx_break">(8)Incorrect semantic generation, missing road markers in the video.
<br class="ltx_break">(9)Wrong decision, changing lanes to the left without slowing down.
<br class="ltx_break">(10)Incorrect semantic generation, unclear ground markings.
<br class="ltx_break"></p>
</div>
</section>
</article>
